question: When the Tamar–Wychwood deal completes, a £220m goodwill entry appears on Tamar's balance sheet. Walk through how that number is built and what happens to it afterwards.
model_answer_md:
Goodwill is the residual of the purchase accounting — the slice of the price that survives every attempt to pin it to a nameable asset.

At completion, Wychwood's balance sheet is restated to fair value: book net assets of £220m, plus a £60m write-up of its brand, gives **£280m** of identifiable net assets. Tamar paid £500m. The unexplained excess is the goodwill:

$$500 - 280 = \mathbf{£220m}$$

It stands for what a healthy business is worth beyond its recorded assets — earning power, workforce, relationships, the synergies Tamar expects — none of which qualifies as a separable asset.

Afterwards, under IFRS, it is **not amortised**. It sits at cost and is tested at least annually for **impairment**: if the acquired business can no longer support the residual, goodwill is written down through the income statement — a non-cash charge, and a public admission of overpayment.

The number it must never be confused with: the premium. Tamar paid £100m over Wychwood's market value but carries £220m of goodwill, because the two are measured against different baselines.
key_points: Residual: price less fair value of identifiable net assets after write-ups
Represents earning power and expected synergies no asset line can hold
Not amortised under IFRS — impairment-tested annually
Distinct from the £100m premium: different baselines, different numbers

follow_ups.question: Why is goodwill not simply amortised away over some period?
follow_ups.answer_md: Because no defensible life exists for it. A well-run acquired business can hold its value indefinitely, so any amortisation schedule would be an arbitrary drag on reported earnings. The impairment regime is meant to be more truthful — the value stays until evidence says it has gone — though it leans on management's own cash-flow forecasts, which is why impairments so often arrive later than the underperformance that caused them.

follow_ups.question: How do goodwill and the premium diverge so widely — £220m against £100m here?
follow_ups.answer_md: They subtract from the £500m price along different baselines. The premium subtracts Wychwood's **market capitalisation** (£400m) — what its equity traded at. Goodwill subtracts its **restated balance sheet** (£280m) — what its identifiable assets are worth. A healthy company's market value normally sits far above its book value, so goodwill normally dwarfs the premium. Buy Wychwood at exactly £400m, no premium at all, and £120m of goodwill would still appear.

weak_answer_note: Calling goodwill the takeover premium, or the value of the brand — the brand write-up is an identifiable intangible and reduces goodwill. Also weak: saying it is amortised.
